title: The farmers' own brand
hook: Middlemen set the price of your milk. What if farmers owned the dairy?
role: You lead the Kaira milk farmers, 1946 to 1973

profit.label: Milk money
profit.hint: What farmers earn from their milk today

future.label: Strength
future.hint: How strong and united the farmers' co-operative is

intro.text: It is 1945, in Kaira district, Gujarat. Your village farmers keep buffaloes, and most families have only one or two litres of milk to sell each day. The government of Bombay has started the Bombay Milk Scheme. Milk travels 427 km from Anand to Bombay. A private dairy, Polson, holds the contract. But no one has fixed the price paid to farmers. The milk contractors pay whatever they like.

d1.title: Who sets the price?
d1.setup: The government makes money from the scheme. Polson keeps a good margin. The contractors take the biggest cut. Farmers get what is left. Milk spoils fast, so they must sell at whatever price they are offered. The freedom leader Sardar Patel has given your farmers advice: build your own co-operative, with your own plant. If the government says no, stop selling milk, even if it hurts for a while.
d1.question: How do you fight for a fair price?
d1.advisor: Milk spoils in hours. Whoever owns the plant decides the price.

options.label: Start village societies, but keep selling to Polson while you talk to the government.
options.outcome: Our estimate: the talks drag on. Farmers keep getting low prices and some lose hope. Your union does start, but later and smaller than it could have been.
options.why: Talking without pressure gave the buyers no reason to change. The farmers stayed weak while you waited.
options.better: Organise every village and be ready to stop supplying. The milk was the only real power the farmers had.
options.takeaway: In 1946 you talked but kept selling. Without pressure, the other side has no reason to move.

options.label: Form a society in every village and one union with its own plant. If the government says no, stop selling milk.
options.outcome: On 4 January 1946, at a meeting in Samarkha village, farmers agreed: every village would form a milk society, and all of them would join one Union that owned its own plant. The government said no. So the farmers went on a milk strike for 15 days. Not a drop of milk was sold to the traders. No milk reached Bombay from Anand, and the Bombay Milk Scheme almost collapsed. The government gave in. Your Union was registered on 14 December 1946.
options.why: Alone, each farmer had no power. Together, and owning the plant, they controlled the milk Bombay needed.
options.takeaway: In 1946 you united the sellers and owned the plant. Together, small farmers had the power one farmer never had.

options.label: Ask the government to fix a fair price, and keep selling through the contractors.
options.outcome: Our estimate: the government promises to look into it. The contractors still decide what farmers get, and a fair price never comes. Farmers start to say that nothing will ever change.
options.why: You asked others to fix your problem and kept the same middlemen. Nothing in the system changed.
options.better: Unite the farmers in their own co-operative, own the plant, and be ready to stop selling.
options.takeaway: In 1946 you asked for a favour instead of building power. A fair deal rarely comes to those who cannot walk away.

text.text: It is June 1948. Your Union starts to pasteurise milk for Bombay. At first it is just two village societies and about 250 litres a day. Any farmer can join, whatever their caste or religion. A sure market is a big pull. By the end of the year 432 farmers have joined, and you handle 5,000 litres a day.
Our estimate: it is 1948. Your union is finally running, but only in a few villages. Farmers who saw the contractors win are slow to trust you, and growth is slow.

d2.title: Too much milk in winter
d2.setup: It is 1953. In winter, buffaloes give about two and a half times more milk than in summer. Bombay cannot take all of it. Your farmers are selling the extra milk cheap to middlemen again. And experts around the world say buffalo milk has too much fat to turn into milk powder.
d2.question: What do you do with the extra winter milk?
d2.advisor: The buffalo does not take a holiday. Your farmers cannot either.

options.label: Take less milk in winter. Tell farmers to keep the extra at home.
options.outcome: Our estimate: farmers pour away milk or sell it cheap to traders. Many stop trusting the union, because it is not there when they need it most.
options.why: A co-operative that turns away its members' milk breaks its main promise: a sure market, every day.
options.better: Find a way to use every litre: make products that keep, like butter and milk powder.
options.takeaway: In 1953 you turned away your members' milk. A promise that only works in good times is not a promise.

options.label: Sell the extra winter milk to private butter makers at whatever price they pay.
options.outcome: Our estimate: the milk gets used, but the private buyers set a low winter price. Farmers earn something, and the middlemen are back in the game.
options.why: It solved this winter, but it handed the price back to the people you had just escaped.
options.better: Build your own factory to turn the extra milk into butter and powder, so the value stays with the farmers.
options.takeaway: In 1953 you sold the surplus cheap. A quick fix can bring back the problem you fought to end.

options.label: Build your own factory to make butter and milk powder, even from buffalo milk.
options.outcome: The government of India helped the Union get money from UNICEF and help from New Zealand, with technical aid from the FAO. A Rs 50 lakh factory for milk powder and butter was planned. The President of India laid its foundation stone on 15 November 1954. In 1955 a dairy engineer at Anand installed the world's first spray-dryer for buffalo milk. Experts had said buffalo milk could not be dried. On 31 October 1955 the Prime Minister opened the factory. Now the Union could take farmers' milk all year round.
options.why: You turned the problem into a product. Milk that went bad in hours became butter and powder that could keep and travel.
options.takeaway: In 1955 you built the plant the experts said could not work, and turned extra milk into products that keep.

text.text: Your new dairy makes butter and milk powder from buffalo milk, a first in the world. You sell them under one name: Amul, from the Sanskrit word 'Amulya', which means priceless. In the years that follow, Amul also makes cheese and baby food from buffalo milk.

Our estimate: after more hard winters, you build a smaller butter plant, years late. You sell under one name, Amul, from the Sanskrit word for priceless. But private dairies already have a head start.

d3.title: Share it with India?

setup.text: It is October 1964. The Prime Minister comes to Anand to open your new cattle feed plant. He spends a night in a village with your farmers. He sees how well it works, and he wants your model copied across India.
Our estimate: it is 1964. Your union is smaller than it could be, but it works. The Prime Minister visits Anand, and he wants farmers across India to have something like it.

d3.question: What do you do with what you have learned?
d3.advisor: One district cannot feed a country. But a good model can travel.

options.label: Help farmers across India build their own co-operatives on the same model.
options.outcome: In 1965 the National Dairy Development Board was set up at Anand to copy the Amul model across India. It later drew up Operation Flood, the biggest dairy program in the world. It was built on what people called the 'Anand Pattern': a society in each village, a union in each district, and a federation in each state.
options.why: You gave away the recipe, not the business. Farmers everywhere got their own co-operatives, and the whole movement grew stronger.
options.takeaway: In 1965 you shared your model with the whole country instead of keeping it for yourself.

options.label: Keep your know-how in Kaira. Farmers in other states are your rivals.
options.outcome: Our estimate: Kaira's farmers do well, but the rest of India stays in the hands of middlemen. Without a national movement, big private dairies grow strong enough to squeeze even you.
options.why: Farmers in other states were not your rivals. The middlemen were. Keeping the model to yourself left you alone.
options.better: Help other farmers build co-operatives of their own, so that farmers, not traders, run India's milk.
options.takeaway: In 1964 you kept a good idea to yourself. A movement grows stronger when it is shared.

options.label: Grow Amul itself: buy milk in other states and run it all from Anand.
options.outcome: Our estimate: Amul grows big, but farmers far away are just suppliers to a dairy in Gujarat. They do not own it, so they do not feel it is theirs.
options.why: Growth helped, but farmers who do not own the dairy have no reason to stay loyal when a trader offers more.
options.better: Let farmers in every state own their own co-operatives on the same model, and link them together.
options.takeaway: In 1964 you grew a company instead of a movement. Ownership is what keeps farmers loyal.

d4.title: Make India love the butter
d4.setup: It is 1966. Amul Butter's ads use an old line: 'Purely the Best'. You want families in every city to ask for Amul by name.
d4.question: How do you sell your butter to India's homes?
d4.advisor: People forget a product. They remember a friend.

options.label: Run plain ads: the price, the purity and a picture of the pack.
options.outcome: Our estimate: the ads are correct and safe. People see them, but they do not talk about them, and the butter still looks like any other brand.
options.why: Plain facts tell people what you sell. They do not make people care.
options.better: Give the brand a face and a voice, something people look forward to seeing.
options.takeaway: In 1966 you ran safe ads. Being correct is not the same as being remembered.

options.label: No ads. Good butter sells itself, and ads waste the farmers' money.
options.outcome: Our estimate: you save money, but big private brands fill the cities with their ads. Shoppers pick the name they know, and it is not yours.
options.why: A good product nobody has heard of loses to an average product everyone knows.
options.better: Spend on a smart, cheap campaign that makes your brand a friend of the family.
options.takeaway: In 1966 you thought quality was enough. Customers can only choose a brand they remember.

options.label: Hire a sharp ad agency for a cheeky campaign, with a little girl who jokes about the news.
options.outcome: In 1966 Amul hired the head of an ad agency to make a new campaign for Amul Butter. He created a little girl mascot to win over mothers and children. Her first topical ad made a joke about horse racing. From 1967 she began to joke about the news of the day, on big roadside boards. The campaign later set a Guinness World Record as the longest-running ad campaign in the world.
options.why: A funny, friendly mascot made a farmers' product feel like part of the family, and the news gave her something new to say every week.
options.takeaway: In 1966 you gave your brand a face and a sense of humour that people looked forward to.

text.text: On 13 January 1970 Operation Flood begins. Its first phase is paid for with milk powder and butter oil given by Europe through the World Food Programme. It links 18 milk areas to Delhi, Bombay, Calcutta and Madras. In Gujarat, other districts like Mehsana, Banaskantha, Baroda, Sabarkantha and Surat have built milk unions just like yours.

Our estimate: it is 1970. In most of India, milk is still run by middlemen. But in Gujarat, other districts like Mehsana, Banaskantha, Baroda, Sabarkantha and Surat have built milk unions of their own.

d5.title: One brand or many?

setup.text: Our estimate: it is 1973. Even without your help, Gujarat's other milk unions have grown. Now they fight with you and with each other in the same towns, each one paying for its own ads.
It is 1973. Gujarat's milk unions all grew from the same idea. But now they compete with each other in the same markets, each one paying for its own ads.

d5.question: How should Gujarat's milk unions sell?
d5.advisor: Farmers fighting farmers is a gift to every big company.

options.label: Let Kaira's Amul win the price war. The other unions can look after themselves.
options.outcome: Our estimate: you cut prices to beat the other unions. Farmers in every district earn less, and private dairies smile as the co-operatives weaken each other.
options.why: Your real competitors were the big private dairies. A war between farmers only made all farmers poorer.
options.better: Join forces: one federation, one brand, one budget, with every union owning a share.
options.takeaway: In 1973 you fought your own allies. Divided farmers are easy to beat.

options.label: Form one marketing federation. Every union sells under one brand: Amul.
options.outcome: In 1973 the unions set up the Gujarat Co-operative Milk Marketing Federation, GCMMF, to sell for all of them. They pooled their strength, cut ad costs and stopped competing with each other. The Kaira Union handed its Amul brand over to the federation. Now farmers owned their village societies, the societies owned the district unions, and the unions owned the federation.
options.why: One brand gave millions of small farmers the power of one big company, while they still owned every part of it.
options.takeaway: In 1973 you gave up your own brand so all farmers could share it. One strong brand beats many weak ones.

options.label: Share trucks and shops, but let each union keep its own brand.
options.outcome: Our estimate: you save some money on trucks, but shoppers see five or six milk names from Gujarat. Each one is too small to stand up to the big brands.
options.why: Sharing costs helped, but the brands still split the shopper's attention and the ad money.
options.better: Put everything under one brand, so every rupee spent on ads helps every farmer.
options.takeaway: In 1973 you shared the trucks but not the name. Saving costs is not the same as building one strong brand.

text.text: In 1976 GCMMF made a film about the milk co-operatives, Manthan. It was paid for by 500,000 farmers, who gave two rupees each. By the end of 1985, 4.25 million milk producers were part of 43,000 village co-operatives. In 1998 India became the largest milk producer in the world. Today 3.6 million milk producers control GCMMF, and Amul is still their brand.
Our estimate: you took a slightly different road, but you kept the farmers united and in charge. Their co-operative grows into one of India's best-known food brands.

survivor.title: A strong local dairy
survivor.text: Our estimate: the farmers keep their union and earn more than in the days of the contractors. But without one strong brand and a national plan, private dairies keep most of India's big city markets.

collapse.title: The middlemen win again
collapse.text: Our estimate: the farmers stay divided, and the middlemen and big dairies win again. Your union shrinks to a small local dairy, and most farmers still sell milk at whatever price they are offered.

fired.title: The farmers choose a new leader
fired.text: Our estimate: after three costly calls, the union's elected board loses its trust in you and chooses someone else to lead the farmers.

realHistory: In 1946 the milk farmers of Kaira, Gujarat, went on a 15-day milk strike and won the right to sell through their own co-operative Union. In 1955 they opened a factory that made milk powder and butter from buffalo milk, a world first, and sold it under the name Amul. From 1965 the National Dairy Development Board copied the model across India through Operation Flood. In 1966 the cheeky Amul girl ads began. In 1973 Gujarat's milk unions formed one federation, GCMMF, to sell under one brand: Amul. By the end of 1985, 4.25 million producers were in 43,000 village co-operatives, and in 1998 India became the world's largest milk producer.
